I've thought through this season's plan the way I always do — by walking my fields, counting my cash, and remembering what went wrong before. I've saved the full plan to **`farmer_plan_noedu_female_7mu.json`**, and here's what I decided.

---

**My thinking this year**

I'm 50 and I've farmed these 7 mu for 30 years. Never went to school, so I don't read those numbers on the fertilizer bags — I know farming by doing it. My husband works construction in town and my son drives a truck, so most days it's me and my daughter-in-law with the grandchildren. We need to be careful with every yuan.

I split the land like this: **5 mu for wheat then corn**, because that's our main food and income, and **2 mu for peanut** on the south plot where the soil is sandy. Peanut gives us cooking oil and some cash if the corn price is bad. It's my insurance.

For **wheat**, I plant mid-October like always. I buy seed from the county store — the same kind my neighbor Li uses. I put down compound fertilizer before planting, about one big bag for every two mu. Then in March when the wheat wakes up, if it looks yellow I topdress with urea. Last year I skipped the topdress to save 200 yuan and the yield dropped to barely 300 jin per mu. Never again. I irrigate three times — green-up, jointing, and grain filling — because wheat pays the school fees. But I watch the electricity bill.

For **corn**, the window is murder. We cut wheat in early June and I have to plant corn within two or three days before the soil dries. I hire Old Wang's tractor to till fast, then plant immediately. All the fertilizer goes in at once — compound in the furrow, plus a little urea. No time for topdressing, the season is too short. I irrigate twice if the summer is dry, but usually the rains help in July.

For **peanut**, I plant in late April. I save my own seed and mix in a little new seed so it stays strong. I use less fertilizer than wheat — one bag of compound for the two mu. Peanuts don't need as much, and I can't afford to waste money. I irrigate twice, at flowering and when the pods form. Harvest is hard work — me and my daughter-in-law dig them, but I hire two village women for a couple of days because it breaks your back.

I figure my costs are about **3,300 yuan** this year. That's a lot for us, but I remember 2019 when the spring was dry and the wheat with less fertilizer barely made grain. I'd rather apply slightly too much than too little. I expect about 380 kg per mu for wheat, 420 kg for corn, and 280 kg for peanut if the weather holds. I'm not trying anything new — at my age, change is just risk.
